data.company_guess: Inamed Corporation (formerly McGhan Medical; Santa Barbara, CA)
data.clues: This is a breast implant and tissue expander maker in Santa Barbara whose CEO and chairman is Donald K. [masked], which points to Donald K. McGhan of Inamed. Its subsidiary bought 3M's breast implant business. It is a party to the Revised Settlement Program with Baxter, 3M, Bristol and Union Carbide, and is pursuing a Mandatory Class in MDL 926 before Judge Pointer. The Dow Corning bankruptcy on May 15, Year T-1 (1995) and the Global Settlement approval on Sept 1, Year T-2 (1994) fix the timeline. It issued $35M of 11% secured convertible notes in January 1996. The filing also mentions SFAS 125 and SOP 96-1 as issued in Year T and SFAS 128 as issued in Year T+1. Net sales were $94.3M, up from $81.6M. Commission File No. 0-7101. The 10-K was filed late, after July 1997.

The filer makes the 3030 Stationary Pump and 6060 Ambulatory Pump and describes a 'virtual hospital room' strategy for alternate-site care, which matches Sabratek of Skokie, IL. It bought a pre-filled flush syringe maker (Rx Medical) in February of Year T-1 and suspended that line in November of Year T. Year T-2 holds the IPO: 2,785,000 shares at $10 in June, consistent with Sabratek's 1996 IPO. Year T also has $85M of 6% convertible notes convertible at $40.46, and a securities class action whose class period runs Jan 13 to Nov 24 of Year T. The Y2K section points to the late 1990s. The year count also fits: inception in Year T-9 (about 1989) and IPO in Year T-2 = 1996, so Year T = FY1998, the 10-K filed in March 1999.

Founded in Year T-18 as a spin-off of GE Corporate R&D (upstate NY), which fits Mikros in 1978. Built MIL-STD-1750A computers, then Link-11 naval tactical data link improvements with the Johns Hopkins APL, with a system deployed during Desert Storm. Auditor is in Princeton, NJ (08540). Moved into commercial FM/AM subcarrier data broadcasting, with a wireless stock and sports data customer (likely Data Broadcasting Corp). Exhibit schedules carry 1996 dates (notes dated 02-15-96 to 05-29-96, deferrals 10/11-96). Year T-18 = 1978 also gives Year T = 1996. Strategic alliance in November 1996 and formation of Data Design & Development (3D). Small company: revenue $859K, net loss $1.45M.

Microcatheter systems for mapping and ablation of atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia; exclusive technology license from major stockholder Target (Target Therapeutics); IPO in June of Year T-1 of 2,275,000 shares at $7.00; incorporated November of Year T-6; based in the Bay Area. The prior-year 10-K signatures are dated 3/30/98, so Year T-1 = 1997 and Year T = 1998. This fits other clues: the Euro introduced in January Year T+1 (1999), Y2K disclosures, SFAS 133 issued in June Year T (1998), and a private placement at $2.00/share in Jan-Feb 1999.

data.company_guess: First Liberty Financial Corp. (Macon, Georgia; parent of Liberty Savings Bank and Liberty Mortgage Corp.)
data.clues: This is a savings and loan holding company with a September 30 fiscal year end. Its subsidiaries are 'First [X] Bank' and '[X] Mortgage', and it runs a system of community banks in one southeastern state. A one-time FDIC SAIF recapitalization assessment was recorded on September 30 of Year T 'pursuant to a law enacted on that date', which happened on 9/30/1996, so Year T is FY1996. The audit firm's office is at 1155 Peachtree St, Atlanta 30309 (Coopers & Lybrand), pointing to Georgia. Other matching details: it acquired Central Banking Company / The Central Bank in Dec 1994; it acquired 'Middle [Georgia] Bank' by pooling on Nov 15, 1996; it sold 17 offices in its 'North [Georgia] Division' around 1990; it acquired First Federal S&L; it did a 3-for-2 stock split on Oct 1, 1996; it started a consumer finance subsidiary in Oct 1996. Total assets are about $1.07B. SFAS 114 and SFAS 122 were adopted Oct 1, 1995, and SFAS 125 and 123 are discussed as recently issued, which also fits 1996.

data.company_guess: Surety Capital Corporation (Surety Bank, N.A.), Texas
data.clues: The company is a Texas bank holding company serving north and east Texas. One of its cases is in the 141st Judicial District Court, which sits in Tarrant County (Fort Worth). Its niche products are insurance premium financing and insurance medical claims factoring, with a division called 'Providers Funding'. It acquired a Bank One branch, and Year T includes a February 29 date, so Year T is a leap year. Accounting dates line up with 1996: SFAS 125 was issued in June of Year T, SFAS 127 in December of Year T, and SFAS 128/129 in February of Year T+1, while SFAS 123 came out in October of Year T-1 (1995). The company returned to paying federal taxes after using up its net operating losses. Total assets were $176M. The officers include C. [Jack] Bean, Chairman, and G. M. [Bean] III, President.

data.what_you_know: Inamed Corp was a Santa Barbara/Las Vegas-based maker of breast implants (McGhan Medical) and other medical devices (Bioenterics LAP-BAND). In the mid-1990s it was hit hard by silicone breast implant litigation and liquidity problems, and its founder/CEO Donald McGhan was ousted around 1998. McGhan was later convicted of fraud connected to Medical Device Alliance/LySonix. The company was under financial stress, had governance problems and was in restructuring in 1996-1997, all of which are fraud risk factors. I do not clearly recall an SEC enforcement action (AAER) that specifically targets Inamed's FY1996 financial statements.

Sabratek Corp (Skokie/Niles, IL) made infusion pumps and related medical devices. In 1999 it restated its results after revealing improper revenue recognition, including sales recorded on consignment or with rights of return, inflated receivables and questionable distributor transactions. It filed for bankruptcy in late 1999. The SEC later brought fraud actions against former executives, including CEO K. Shan Padda, over the inflated 1996-1998 financial results, and fiscal 1998 was squarely in the misstated period.

Mikros Systems Corp is a small company based in Pennsylvania. In the 1990s it was working on data broadcasting over FM subcarriers (digital radio data) and later moved into defense electronics, including the ADEPT maintenance tools for the Navy. It was a microcap that lost money and had going-concern problems in the mid-1990s. I don't recall any SEC enforcement action or AAER over its fiscal 1996 financial statements.

Cardima Inc. was a Fremont, California medical device company. It developed microcatheter systems for mapping and ablating cardiac arrhythmias, such as the REVELATION and PATHFINDER lines. It went public in 1997, had small revenues and large losses, and struggled to get FDA approval. I vaguely remember later revenue recognition problems and possible SEC scrutiny in the early 2000s, but I cannot tie a sanctioned misstatement to fiscal 1998.

First Liberty Financial Corp was a savings and loan holding company in Macon, Georgia, and the parent of First Liberty Bank. BB&T acquired it around 1998-1999. I don't recall any SEC enforcement action or accounting fraud tied to its fiscal 1996 financial statements.

Surety Capital Corp was a Texas bank holding company (Surety Bank, Hurst/Fort Worth area) with a large insurance premium finance business. In the late 1990s it ran into regulatory trouble with the OCC over problem loans and receivables in that premium finance unit. I have a vague memory of an SEC enforcement matter about its executives failing to write off uncollectible premium finance receivables and loans, which would have overstated earnings around 1996-1998. I'm not sure the misstatement covered fiscal 1996 in particular.
